case_study_insert.main_stem: Pinecrest Leisure Parks (PLP) is a public limited company in the leisure and visitor-attraction sector, employing a workforce of 225. Founded in 1996 by Grace Oyelaran, it operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership and sells 45,000 units a year, one unit being a park admission at an average selling price of $75. PLP plans to invest $1,500,000 in a new water-slide complex and splash zone, financed by a $900,000 bank loan and a $600,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $750,000 a year and a variable cost of $25 a unit. Average queue times at three popular rides have reached 42 minutes and food-outlet waste has risen to 6.4% of purchases.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report, Q2 2025: PLP welcomed 11,250 admissions with 63 complaint logs, up from 41 last year, while average queue time at the three busiest rides reached 42 minutes against a 20-minute target. Food-outlet waste was 6.4% of purchases. A visitor survey of 1,050 families found 74% would pay $8 more for a fast-track water-slide ticket and 59% choose parks with short queues. Of 225 staff, 44 ride operators have not completed on-the-job queue-management training; off-the-job customer-service courses at the regional college cost $410 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Pinecrest Leisure Parks as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Family-Leisure Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, increasing the cost of PLP's variable-rate $900,000 bank loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.9% from $14.21 to $15.05 an hour from April 2026, affecting ride and catering staff. (3) Park energy costs have risen 10.8%, family day-trip spending grew 3.7% and consumer inflation is 5.1%.

questions.question_text: PLP plans to fund part of its water-slide complex with a $900,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for PLP of using the $600,000 share issue instead of borrowing more.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue provides permanent capital with no interest charges and no fixed repayment dates, so PLP can commit the $600,000 to the water-slide complex without increasing the burden of its $900,000 bank loan at a time when the base rate has risen to 5.0%. With fixed costs of $750,000 a year and energy costs up 10.8%, avoiding extra debt service protects the $50 contribution earned on each of the 45,000 admissions and leaves cash to tackle the 42-minute queues.

Point 2: Equity does not require the park's land and rides to be offered as collateral, so the $1,500,000 development does not put existing assets at risk if the new attraction underperforms — a genuine concern while complaints have risen to 63 and 6.4% of food purchases are wasted. As a public limited company, PLP can raise the $600,000 from investors and strengthen its balance sheet before borrowing the remaining $900,000. The cost is dilution of shareholders including founder Grace Oyelaran, but for a long-life attraction that will earn revenue for years, permanent share capital is better matched than short-term debt.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to PLP's funding and attraction investment.

questions.question_text: PLP is promoting its new water-slide complex. Consider local television advertising, regional radio advertising, and social media family influencers. Which should PLP choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local television advertising: Regional TV can show the water slides in action to a large family audience and build awareness of the $1,500,000 complex quickly, supporting the 74% of surveyed families who would pay $8 more for a fast-track ticket. However, airtime is expensive while PLP services a $900,000 loan and $750,000 fixed costs, and much of the audience lies outside the park's day-trip catchment, so a large part of the spend would be wasted.

Regional radio advertising: Local radio is cheaper and can reach nearby families with short-notice messages about the new splash zone, with flexible scheduling around school holidays. Its weakness is that sound cannot show the slides, and it does not reach families who plan theme-park trips in advance from further afield, so on its own it is unlikely to generate the 45,000 admissions needed.

Social media family influencers: Parenting and family-travel influencers can show the water-slide complex visually to the 59% of surveyed families who choose parks with short queues and the 74% who would pay $8 more for fast track. Content is shareable, targeting is precise and engagement is measurable, though results build gradually and depend on credible influencers.

Recommendation: PLP should choose social media family influencers, supported by limited local radio close to opening. Influencers show the attraction and reach the queue-conscious, experience-seeking families who justify the $1,500,000 investment, at a cost controllable from the $600,000 share issue. Local television is rejected as costly and geographically wasteful while the park carries a $900,000 loan; radio alone is rejected because it cannot display the slides or drive advance bookings from beyond the immediate area. Influencer material can be repurposed across channels for better value.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the promotional options with minimal application to PLP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of PLP with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of PLP with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: PLP faces 42-minute queues and 6.4% food-outlet waste. Explain two benefits for PLP of its democratic leadership style in addressing these problems.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership invites ideas from the workforce of 225, including the ride operators who see the 42-minute queues every day. Staff suggestions on queue layout, staggered entry and pre-booked time slots can be tried quickly, helping move towards the 20-minute target and addressing the 59% of families who choose parks with short queues. Because those who implement the changes help design them, the solutions are more practical and more readily accepted on the ground.

Point 2: Involving food-outlet teams in decisions can generate ways to cut the 6.4% waste, such as better portion planning or reusing unsold stock within food-safety rules, protecting the $50 contribution per admission. Participation also raises job satisfaction and commitment across 225 staff, which matters when the minimum wage rises 5.9% to $15.05 and PLP needs productivity from its ride and catering teams to fund the $1,500,000 water-slide complex. Democratic leadership therefore attacks both the queue problem and waste through front-line ideas while supporting morale.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to PLP's queues, waste and expansion.

questions.question_text: PLP must train 44 ride operators in queue management. Consider on-the-job training and off-the-job customer-service courses at the regional college. Which should PLP choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching the 44 untrained operators at the rides uses PLP's own queue system and real peak-time conditions, so training targets the 42-minute waits directly and staff stay at their posts. It costs no course fees, protecting cash while the park services a $900,000 loan, and supervisors can correct bottlenecks as they happen. Its drawback is that trainers are working operators whose own duties suffer, and inconsistent coaching across rides could leave the 63 complaints unresolved.

Off-the-job training: The regional college customer-service course at $410 per employee gives structured queue-management and communication skills plus a recognised certificate for all 44 operators, costing 44 × $410 = $18,040 — small beside the $1,500,000 complex and affordable from the $600,000 share issue. It removes staff from the rides for several days, however, which could lengthen queues further during busy periods, and generic content may not match PLP's specific ride procedures without on-site follow-up.

Decision: PLP should choose on-the-job training as the main approach, with short college modules for senior operators. On-the-job training tackles the 42-minute queues using the park's own system, keeps all rides staffed and avoids the $18,040 fee at a time when waste and complaints are already problems. Full off-the-job training now is rejected because taking 44 operators off the rides would worsen the very queues the park is trying to reduce; college modules can be added in the off-peak season once the water-slide complex opens. PLP should monitor complaint logs and average queue times afterwards so that the $18,040, if later spent, can be justified by a measurable fall in the 42-minute waits.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to PLP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both methods in the context of PLP.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods with a well-justified decision covering cost, ride cover and operational relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how PLP's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $750,000 ÷ ($75 − $25) = $750,000 ÷ $50 = 15,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 15,000 park admissions a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $75 − $25 = $50. Answer: contribution per unit is $50.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways PLP's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 15,000-unit break-even output with 45,000 admissions: PLP has a margin of safety of 45,000 − 15,000 = 30,000 units, showing the visitor fall it could absorb before failing to cover $750,000 fixed costs, helpful while queues are long.
2. Use contribution per unit of $50 to evaluate the $8 fast-track ticket: it would lift contribution towards $58, indicating the extra revenue available to service the $900,000 bank loan.
3. Set targets for the $1,500,000 water-slide complex: 30,000 extra admissions at $50 contribution generate $1,500,000, so managers can track how fast the investment is recovered.
4. Benchmark average total cost of $750,000 ÷ 45,000 + $25 = $41.67 an admission and labour productivity of 45,000 ÷ 225 = 200 admissions per employee, a baseline for measuring the 10.8% energy rise and the effect of food waste of 6.4%.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 15,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $50 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 30,000 admissions; $8 fast-track pricing analysis; target volume for the $1,500,000 complex; and unit-cost benchmarking at $41.67 with labour productivity of 200 admissions per employee.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate PLP's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has PLP's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.01 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.30 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.78 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.05 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $48,000 inventories + $70,000 trade receivables + $90,000 cash = $208,000; 2025 current assets = $55,000 + $105,000 + $120,000 = $280,000. Coverage of short-term obligations 2024 = $208,000 ÷ $205,000 = 1.01; 2025 = $280,000 ÷ $215,000 = 1.30. Excluding stock: 2024 = ($208,000 − $48,000) ÷ $205,000 = $160,000 ÷ $205,000 = 0.78; 2025 = ($280,000 − $55,000) ÷ $215,000 = $225,000 ÷ $215,000 = 1.05.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved clearly. Coverage of short-term obligations rose from 1.01 to 1.30 because current assets grew by $72,000 while current liabilities increased only $10,000 to $215,000. The stock-excluding measure improved from 0.78 to 1.05, so PLP can now cover its short-term debts from cash and receivables without selling food and merchandise stock — useful while it services a $900,000 loan and builds a $1,500,000 complex. Cash rose from $90,000 to $120,000 and receivables from $70,000 to $105,000. The rise in receivables is the main caution: if tour operators and corporate bookings pay late, part of this apparent strength could reverse, so credit control should be watched.

Conclusion: PLP's financial position has improved. Both measures are higher in 2025, and the move from 0.78 to 1.05 in the stock-excluding measure is the stronger evidence of better underlying liquidity. PLP should keep an eye on receivables but can fund the water-slide complex from a healthier short-term position.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of cash, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion that liquidity improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for PLP of introducing the $8 fast-track water-slide ticket backed by 74% of surveyed families.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: An $8 fast-track ticket turns the 42-minute queue problem into a revenue opportunity: the 74% of 1,050 surveyed families who would pay $8 more lift contribution per admission from $50 towards $58, helping cover $750,000 fixed costs and the $900,000 loan. It also directly answers the 59% who choose parks with short queues, improving satisfaction while the 63 complaints are being reduced and supporting the $1,500,000 water-slide investment.

Disadvantage: A paid fast lane creates a two-tier experience in which standard ticket holders face relatively longer waits, which could raise complaints further if the 42-minute queues are not also tackled operationally. The 74% figure is stated willingness to pay, not guaranteed purchases, so revenue may fall short. Introducing separate lanes may need extra staffing from a workforce of 225, adding cost when the 5.9% wage rise and 10.8% energy inflation are already squeezing the $25 variable cost per admission; PLP must therefore improve ordinary queue times too.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to PLP's survey, queues and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 5.9% minimum wage increase and the 10.8% rise in park energy costs will affect PLP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): If PLP's $900,000 bank loan follows the base rate, the extra interest is 0.75% of $900,000 = $6,750 a year (0.0075 × $900,000). This is a small fraction of the $750,000 fixed costs and can be largely avoided by fixing the rate. Higher borrowing costs could raise the price of future finance for the $1,500,000 complex, but the direct annual effect is modest.

Minimum wage increase (5.9%, to $15.05 an hour): Ride and catering staff are hourly paid, so this rise increases PLP's wage bill across the workforce of 225 and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so an annual total cannot be invented; the defensible judgement is qualitative against the given 200 admissions per employee and $50 contribution per unit. With queues at 42 minutes and waste at 6.4%, productivity must hold if the wage rise is to be absorbed without raising the $75 price.

Park energy costs (10.8%): These affect the whole park and every one of the 45,000 admissions. The insert does not break down the $25 variable cost, so only a bound can be calculated honestly: if the whole variable cost rose 10.8%, that is 10.8% × $25 = $2.70 a unit, or about $121,500 a year (45,000 × $2.70). Even a smaller rise would cut into the $50 contribution needed to repay the loan and fund the water-slide complex, with only partial recovery through the $8 fast-track ticket.

Conclusion: The 10.8% rise in park energy costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 45,000 admissions and directly erodes the $50 contribution underpinning the $1,500,000 investment, whereas the interest rise is modest and can be hedged by fixing the loan rate, and the wage rise can be offset through productivity and pricing. Energy inflation therefore calls for the most urgent response, such as efficiency investment and longer-term supply contracts.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to PLP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on PLP's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in the context of PLP with a well-justified judgement that energy-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
